source.citation: M. Allen Starr, "Clinic on Nervous Diseases, Held at the Vanderbilt Clinic, March 24, 1888: Lead Paralysis," Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease 15 (1888): 452–454.

complaints: weakness beginning in the shoulder; cannot lift the arm
presentation.course: Seven weeks; somewhat better than at the start. No pain, numbness, or tingling.

findings: well nourished but anaemic and pale
right arm cannot be abducted; left only partly; scapular rotation normal, so the deltoid is at fault
marked tremor with the arms held out
grip seems weak, but is strong once the wrist is held extended
reaction of degeneration in the right deltoid, partial on the left; biceps normal
quotes: painters who work within buildings, and especially those who work in close rooms, are more liable to develop lead poisoning

modernReading.text: Lead neuropathy, mainly motor, affecting the radial-nerve muscles and the deltoids, after occupational exposure to lead paint. Anaemia and colic fit the same cause.

constrained.rule: indoor lead exposure: house or carriage painter, varnisher, type founder, stereotyper, white-lead worker, file cutter

notes: Teaching-clinic demonstration. The excerpt gives no treatment or outcome; the condition table must supply them. Samuel Taylor draws on the same condition.
